title: JS for ServiceNow: 2. GlideRecord Basics
excerpt: Master the most important API in ServiceNow. Learn to query, create, update, and delete records with real interview scenarios and execution traces.
content:
The Foundation of Everything

GlideRecord is the single most important skill for ServiceNow development and the primary API for server-side database operations. It enables querying, creating, updating, and deleting records across any table, making it the core interface between your scripts and the ServiceNow database.

The GlideRecord API is a server-side JavaScript object that represents records from tables like incident, problem, or sys_user. It provides methods to add query conditions, execute database hits, iterate results, and perform CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete). Unlike client-side scripting, this API runs on the server for secure, efficient data access.

🎯 INTERVIEW SCENARIO: "Write a script that finds all active high-priority incidents assigned to the 'Network' group and updates their state to 'In Progress' if they've been open for more than 24 hours."

WHAT THEY'RE TESTING: Query construction, date comparisons, efficient updates, and understanding of when conditions.

GlideRecord API Overview

The GlideRecord API supports both global and scoped applications. In global scope, use new GlideRecord('table_name'). In scoped apps, it respects application access controls. Key categories include:

  • Query Methods: addQuery(), addEncodedQuery(), query(), get()
  • CRUD Methods: initialize(), insert(), update(), deleteRecord(), deleteMultiple()
  • Iteration Methods: next(), hasNext()
  • Utility Methods: setValue(), getValue(), setLimit()

Basic Query Pattern

Every GlideRecord interaction follows: Create → Configure → Query → Iterate.

// === CREATE: Initialize GlideRecord on a table ===
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');

// === CONFIGURE: Add your conditions ===
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.addQuery('priority', 1);
gr.addQuery('assignment_group', 'Network Group Sys ID');
// Open for more than 24 hours

gr.addQuery('sys_created_on', '<=', gs.hoursAgoStart(24));

// === QUERY: Execute the database query ===
gr.query();

// === ITERATE: Loop through results ===
while (gr.next()) {
  gr.setValue('state', 2); // In Progress
  gr.update();
  gs.info('Updated: ' + gr.getValue('number'));
}

Execution Trace

StepWhat HappensDatabase Impact
new GlideRecord('incident')Creates object pointing to incident tableNone yet
addQuery(...)Builds WHERE conditionsNone yet
query()Executes SELECT with your conditionsDatabase hit
next()Moves pointer to next recordNone
update()Persists changeDatabase write

The get() Shortcut

Use get() for single records by sys_id or unique field—it's faster than query() for one record.

// By sys_id (most common)
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (gr.get('a1b2c3d4e5f6...')) {
  gs.info('Found: ' + gr.getValue('number'));
}

// By any unique field
var userGr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
if (userGr.get('user_name', 'admin')) {
  gs.info('Admin sys_id: ' + userGr.getUniqueValue());
}

Creating Records

The GlideRecord API's insert() method creates new records after setting fields via initialize() and setValue().

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.initialize();
gr.setValue('short_description', 'Network outage in Building A');
gr.setValue('category', 'network');
gr.setValue('priority', 2);
var newSysId = gr.insert();

gs.info('Created incident: ' + newSysId);

Updating Records

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (gr.get('number', 'INC0010001')) {
  gr.setValue('state', 2);
  gr.setValue('assigned_to', gs.getUserID());
  gr.update();
}

Deleting Records

deleteRecord() removes the current record; deleteMultiple() bulk-deletes matching ones.

// Delete single record
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (gr.get('sys_id_here')) {
  gr.deleteRecord();
}

// Delete multiple records
var gr2 = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr2.addQuery('state', 7);
gr2.addQuery('sys_created_on', '<', gs.daysAgo(365));
gr2.deleteMultiple();

Essential Query Operators

OperatorExampleMeaning
=addQuery('priority', 1)Equals
!=addQuery('state', '!=', 6)Not equals
>addQuery('priority', '>', 2)Greater than
INaddQuery('state', 'IN', '1,2,3')In list
CONTAINSaddQuery('short_description', 'CONTAINS', 'network')Contains text
ISEMPTYaddQuery('assigned_to', 'ISEMPTY')Field is empty

Performance: setLimit()

💡 Always use setLimit() when you only need a few records:
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.setLimit(10);
gr.query();
This prevents querying millions of records and improves performance.

Advanced GlideRecord API Features

Key methods include addEncodedQuery() for complex filters, clearQuery() to reset conditions, and hasNext() for pre-checking results.

// Complex encoded query
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addEncodedQuery('active=true^priority=1^sys_created_on<javascript:gs.daysAgo(1)');
gr.query();
while (gr.hasNext()) {
  gr.next();
  gs.print(gr.getValue('number'));
}

Challenge: Put It All Together

🏋️ CHALLENGE: Write a script that:
1. Finds all incidents in "New" state (state=1)
2. Open for more than 48 hours (use gs.hoursAgoStart(48))
3. No assigned user (assigned_to ISEMPTY)
4. Updates priority to 2 (High)

Solution:
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('state', 1);
gr.addQuery('sys_created_on', '<=', gs.hoursAgoStart(48));
gr.addQuery('assigned_to', 'ISEMPTY');
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
  gr.setValue('priority', 2);
  gr.update();
}

Mastering the GlideRecord API unlocks efficient database interactions in ServiceNow, from background scripts to business rules.

title: JS for ServiceNow: 3. Business Rules
excerpt: Learn when and how to use Business Rules effectively. Understand before vs after rules, avoid common pitfalls, and master the 'current' and 'previous' objects.
content:
The Heart of Server-Side Logic

Business Rules are scripts that run when records are inserted, updated, deleted, or queried. They're the most powerful—and most commonly misused—server-side scripting tool in ServiceNow.

🎯 INTERVIEW SCENARIO: "An incident's priority should automatically escalate to P1 if it remains unassigned for more than 4 hours. How would you implement this?"

WHAT THEY'RE TESTING: Understanding of rule timing, when to use scheduled jobs vs business rules, and efficient database operations.

When Do Business Rules Run?

TypeWhen It RunsUse Case
BeforeBefore record is saved to databaseValidate data, set default values, modify current record
AfterAfter record is saved to databaseUpdate related records, send notifications, create tasks
AsyncAfter save, in backgroundHeavy processing, external API calls
DisplayWhen form loads (query)Set up client-side variables (g_scratchpad)

The 'current' and 'previous' Objects

// 'current' = the record being saved (with new values)
// 'previous' = the record before changes (read-only)

// Example: Detect if priority changed
if (current.priority.changesTo(1)) {
  gs.info('Priority escalated to P1!');
}

// Example: Detect any change to a field
if (current.state.changes()) {
  gs.info('State changed from ' + previous.state + ' to ' + current.state);
}

Execution Trace: Before Rule

Stepcurrent.stateprevious.stateDatabase
User clicks Save3 (new value)1 (old value)Still has 1
Before rule runs31Still has 1
Rule modifies currentModified1Still has 1
After rule completes--NOW saves current

Before Rule Example: Auto-Set Assignment Group

🎯 SCENARIO: When a user selects a Category of "Network", automatically set the Assignment Group to "Network Support".
// Business Rule: Auto-assign Network Incidents
// Table: incident
// When: before insert, before update
// Condition: current.category.changesTo('network')

(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  var groupGr = new GlideRecord('sys_user_group');
  groupGr.addQuery('name', 'Network Support');
  groupGr.query();

  if (groupGr.next()) {
    current.assignment_group = groupGr.getUniqueValue();
  }
})(current, previous);

After Rule Example: Create Follow-up Task

🎯 SCENARIO: When an incident is resolved, automatically create a follow-up task for customer satisfaction survey.
// Business Rule: Create Survey Task on Resolution
// Table: incident
// When: after update
// Condition: current.state.changesTo(6)

(function executeRule(current, previous) {
  var task = new GlideRecord('task');
  task.initialize();
  task.short_description = 'Customer survey for ' + current.number;
  task.parent = current.getUniqueValue();
  task.assigned_to = current.assigned_to;
  task.description = 'Please contact customer to complete satisfaction survey.';
  task.insert();

  gs.info('Created follow-up task for ' + current.number);
})(current, previous);

Condition Field vs Script Conditions

ApproachWhen to Use
Condition field: current.priority == 1Simple field comparisons
Script: if (complexLogic()) {...}Multiple conditions, lookups, calculations
💡 Performance Tip: Put as much logic as possible in the Condition field. It's evaluated before the script even loads, saving processing time when conditions aren't met.

Preventing Recursion

// Use setWorkflow(false) to prevent Business Rules from triggering on your update
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (gr.get(relatedIncidentId)) {
  gr.setWorkflow(false);
  gr.autoSysFields(false);
  gr.setValue('state', 6);
  gr.update();
}

Business Rules are the workhorse of ServiceNow automation. Master them, and you'll unlock the platform's true power.

title: JS for ServiceNow: 4. Script Includes
excerpt: Build reusable code libraries with Script Includes. Learn the difference between classless and class-based includes, and when to use client-callable scripts.
content:
Write Once, Use Everywhere

Script Includes are reusable server-side code libraries. Instead of copying the same code into multiple Business Rules, you write it once in a Script Include and call it from anywhere.

🎯 INTERVIEW SCENARIO: "Your team has the same incident validation logic duplicated across 5 Business Rules. How would you refactor this?"

WHAT THEY'RE TESTING: Understanding of code reusability, Script Include patterns, and maintainability best practices.

Two Common Styles of Script Includes

1) Class-Based (Recommended for most production use)

// Script Include: IncidentHelper
// Accessible from: Server-side only

var IncidentHelper = Class.create();
IncidentHelper.prototype = {
  initialize: function(incidentGr) {
    this.incident = incidentGr;
  },

  isHighPriority: function() {
    return parseInt(this.incident.getValue('priority'), 10) <= 2;
  },

  getAssignmentGroupName: function() {
    var group = this.incident.assignment_group.getRefRecord();
    return group.isValidRecord() ? group.getValue('name') : 'Unassigned';
  },

  escalate: function(reason) {
    this.incident.setValue('priority', 1);
    this.incident.setValue('work_notes', 'Escalated: ' + reason);
    return this.incident.update();
  },

  type: 'IncidentHelper'
};

Usage in Business Rule:

var helper = new IncidentHelper(current);
if (helper.isHighPriority() && current.assigned_to.nil()) {
  helper.escalate('High priority and unassigned');
}

2) Simple Utility (Ok for small helpers)

// Script Include: IncidentUtils
// Pattern: expose a single object with functions

var IncidentUtils = {
  isVIPUser: function(userId) {
    var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
    return gr.get(userId) && gr.getValue('vip') == 'true';
  },

  getActiveIncidentCount: function(userId) {
    var ga = new GlideAggregate('incident');
    ga.addQuery('assigned_to', userId);
    ga.addQuery('active', true);
    ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
    ga.query();
    return ga.next() ? parseInt(ga.getAggregate('COUNT'), 10) : 0;
  }
};

Client-Callable Script Includes (GlideAjax)

When you mark a Script Include as Client callable, it is typically written by extending AbstractAjaxProcessor. Client scripts call named methods using sysparm_name and parameters using sysparm_*.

// Script Include: UserUtilsAjax
// Client callable: true

var UserUtilsAjax = Class.create();
UserUtilsAjax.prototype = Object.extendsObject(AbstractAjaxProcessor, {
  getUserEmail: function() {
    var userId = this.getParameter('sysparm_user_id');
    var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
    return (gr.get(userId) && gr.email) ? gr.getValue('email') : '';
  },

  type: 'UserUtilsAjax'
});

Client Script Usage:

var ga = new GlideAjax('UserUtilsAjax');
ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'getUserEmail');
ga.addParam('sysparm_user_id', g_form.getValue('caller_id'));
ga.getXMLAnswer(function(answer) {
  g_form.setValue('u_caller_email', answer);
});

Best Practices for Script Includes

  • Single Responsibility: Each Script Include should do one thing well
  • Validation: Validate inputs and return predictable outputs
  • Security: Keep client-callable includes minimal; enforce ACL-friendly access
  • Performance: Avoid repeated queries; cache where appropriate
  • Naming: Use clear names that describe behavior, not implementation

Script Includes are your foundation for writing maintainable, scalable ServiceNow code. Master this pattern and your development speed will multiply.

title: JS for ServiceNow: 5. GlideAjax and Client-Server Communication
excerpt: Learn how to communicate between client-side scripts and server-side code using GlideAjax. Understand asynchronous patterns and real-time data fetching.
content:
Bridge the Client-Server Gap

GlideAjax is ServiceNow's mechanism for making asynchronous calls from client-side scripts to server-side Script Includes. This is essential for real-time validations, lookups, and dynamic UI updates without page reloads.

🎯 INTERVIEW SCENARIO: "When a user selects a caller on an incident, you need to populate their email address, department, and manager name in real-time. How would you implement this without a page refresh?"

WHAT THEY'RE TESTING: Async patterns, callback functions, and understanding of client vs server scope.

The GlideAjax Pattern

Every GlideAjax call follows four steps: Create instance, Add parameters, Define callback, Execute.

Server-Side Script Include

// Script Include: CallerInfoAjax
// Client callable: true

var CallerInfoAjax = Class.create();
CallerInfoAjax.prototype = Object.extendsObject(AbstractAjaxProcessor, {
  getUserInfo: function() {
    var userId = this.getParameter('sysparm_user_id');
    var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
    if (gr.get(userId)) {
      var result = {
        email: gr.getValue('email'),
        department: gr.getDisplayValue('department'),
        manager: gr.getDisplayValue('manager'),
        phone: gr.getValue('phone')
      };
      return JSON.stringify(result);
    }
    return JSON.stringify({ error: 'User not found' });
  },

  type: 'CallerInfoAjax'
});

Client-Side onChange Script

// Client Script: onChange (caller_id)
function onChange(control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading) {
  if (isLoading || !newValue) return;

  var ga = new GlideAjax('CallerInfoAjax');
  ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'getUserInfo');
  ga.addParam('sysparm_user_id', newValue);

  ga.getXMLAnswer(function(answer) {
    var data = JSON.parse(answer || '{}');
    if (data.error) {
      g_form.showFieldMsg('caller_id', data.error, 'error');
      return;
    }

    g_form.setValue('u_caller_email', data.email || '');
    g_form.setValue('u_caller_dept', data.department || '');
    g_form.setValue('u_caller_manager', data.manager || '');
    g_form.setValue('u_caller_phone', data.phone || '');
  });
}

Execution Trace: GlideAjax Call

EventScopeWhat HappensTime
User changes callerClientonChange firesT+0ms
Create GlideAjaxClientRequest is preparedT+5ms
getXMLAnswer()ClientHTTP request sentT+10ms
Script Include runsServerReads sys_user and returns JSONT+50ms
Callback executesClientFields updatedT+100ms

Common GlideAjax Patterns

Pattern 1: Simple Lookup

var ga = new GlideAjax('SomeAjax');
ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'lookup');
ga.addParam('sysparm_key', 'value');
ga.getXMLAnswer(function(response) {
  // handle response
});

Pattern 2: With Error Handling

var ga = new GlideAjax('ValidationAjax');
ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'validate');
ga.addParam('sysparm_value', g_form.getValue('u_field'));

ga.getXMLAnswer(function(response) {
  if (response == 'ERROR') {
    g_form.showFieldMsg('u_field', 'Validation failed', 'error');
  }
});

GlideAjax is your gateway to creating responsive, real-time ServiceNow interfaces. Master this pattern for seamless user experiences.

title: JS for ServiceNow: 6. Advanced Optimization Patterns
excerpt: Learn performance optimization techniques including N+1 query prevention, caching strategies, and efficient bulk operations.
content:
Write Fast Code That Scales

The difference between code that works and code that scales is attention to performance. This section covers real patterns used in production ServiceNow instances handling millions of records.

🎯 INTERVIEW SCENARIO: "Your Business Rule that updates related incidents is causing database timeouts when processing 50,000 incidents daily. How would you optimize it?"

WHAT THEY'RE TESTING: Understanding of N+1 queries, batch processing, and GlideRecord efficiency.

Anti-Pattern: The N+1 Query Problem

Bad: This code queries incidents, then AGAIN for each incident's group:

// ❌ INEFFICIENT: N+1 Query
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.query();

while (gr.next()) {
  var groupGr = new GlideRecord('sys_user_group');
  groupGr.get(gr.assignment_group);
  gs.info('Incident ' + gr.number + ' assigned to ' + groupGr.name);
}
// Total hits: 1 + number of incidents

Solution: Caching

Good: Cache group names so each group is queried once:

// ✅ OPTIMIZED: Cached Lookups
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.query();

var groupCache = {};

while (gr.next()) {
  var groupId = gr.getValue('assignment_group');

  if (groupId && !groupCache[groupId]) {
    var groupGr = new GlideRecord('sys_user_group');
    if (groupGr.get(groupId)) {
      groupCache[groupId] = groupGr.getValue('name');
    }
  }

  gs.info('Incident ' + gr.getValue('number') + ' assigned to ' + (groupCache[groupId] || 'Unassigned'));
}

Bulk Operations: Know When updateMultiple Works

If you are setting the same value on many records, updateMultiple() is usually faster than looping.

// ✅ FAST: One update statement (same values for all matches)
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('priority', 5);
gr.setValue('priority', 3);
gr.updateMultiple();

Query Optimization: Essential Techniques

1. Use setLimit() for Large Tables

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.setLimit(1000);
gr.query();

2. Use orderBy() for Pagination

var pageSize = 100;
var offset = 0;

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.orderBy('sys_created_on');
gr.setSkip(offset);
gr.setLimit(pageSize);
gr.query();

3. Use addEncodedQuery() for Complex Filters

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addEncodedQuery('active=true^priority<=3^assignment_group!=NULL');
gr.query();

GlideAggregate for Reporting

Never use GlideRecord + loop for counting:

// ✅ GOOD: Database does the counting
var ga = new GlideAggregate('incident');
ga.addQuery('active', true);
ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
ga.query();
if (ga.next()) {
  gs.info('Total incidents: ' + ga.getAggregate('COUNT'));
}

Conclusion

Performance optimization in ServiceNow is mostly about reducing database hits, avoiding heavy loops, and choosing the right API for the job. Start by eliminating N+1 queries, then move to caching and bulk operations. Small fixes in one script can save minutes (or hours) across a day of platform load.

title: ServiceNow ITSM Automation: CMDB Best Practices and Workflow Optimization
excerpt: Discover essential best practices for automating ITSM in ServiceNow, focusing on maintaining an accurate CMDB for better decision-making and optimizing workflows with Flow Designer for efficiency.
content:
Introduction to ITSM Automation in ServiceNow

ServiceNow ITSM automation transforms IT service management by leveraging ITIL best practices, enabling organizations to streamline processes, reduce manual efforts, and enhance service delivery through tools like Flow Designer for workflow optimization and a well-maintained CMDB for informed decision-making.

CMDB Best Practices for ITSM Excellence

The Configuration Management Database (CMDB) acts as the foundational repository for IT assets and their relationships, powering effective incident, change, and problem management while supporting automation across ITSM processes.

  • Maintain Data Accuracy: Conduct regular audits and updates of Configuration Item (CI) records to ensure they accurately reflect real-world asset relationships and dependencies.
  • Leverage Integrations: Integrate ServiceNow with discovery tools like ServiceNow Discovery to automate data synchronization, keeping the CMDB current without manual intervention.
  • Implement Relationships: Define precise horizontal and vertical relationships between CIs to visualize impact analysis and enable proactive issue resolution during incidents or changes.
  • Adopt ITIL Alignment: Structure the CMDB according to ITIL configuration management practices, using classes like cmdb_ci_server or cmdb_ci_network_gear for standardized data modeling.

This script example demonstrates querying the CMDB to associate an incident with its affected CI:

var incident = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (incident.get(current.getValue('sys_id'))) {
  var cmdbCi = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci');
  cmdbCi.addQuery('name', incident.affected_ci);
  cmdbCi.query();
  if (cmdbCi.next()) {
    incident.cmdb_ci = cmdbCi.sys_id;
    incident.update();
  }
}

An accurate CMDB directly enhances automation by providing reliable data for Flow Designer triggers and actions, such as routing incidents based on CI ownership.

Introduction to Flow Designer for Workflow Automation

Flow Designer is ServiceNow's no-code, drag-and-drop tool for building scalable automations, replacing legacy Workflow Editor with intuitive components like triggers, actions, subflows, and spokes to optimize ITSM workflows efficiently.

Key components include:

  • Triggers: Define when a flow starts, such as record creation on the Incident table with conditions like high priority.
  • Actions: Reusable steps like Create Record, Send Email, or Ask for Approval, sourced from core actions or application-specific spokes like ITSM Spoke.
  • Subflows: Modular, reusable sequences of actions that promote maintainability across multiple parent flows.
  • Data Pills: Drag-and-drop references to action outputs, ensuring flows adapt dynamically without breaking scripts.

Flow Designer supports spokes—scoped applications with pre-built actions for tables like Incident or Problem—activated via plugins or the ServiceNow Store for extended ITSM capabilities.

Optimizing Workflows with Flow Designer Best Practices

Workflow optimization in ServiceNow leverages Flow Designer's modular architecture to create efficient, error-resilient automations tailored for ITSM, from incident routing to change approvals.

  • Migrate from Legacy Workflows: Convert existing workflows to Flow Designer using built-in tools, starting with Utah release features that refactor actions into subflows automatically for better scalability.
  • Use Modular Subflows: Build department-specific subflows, like IT provisioning or HR onboarding, passing record references instead of multiple inputs to reduce complexity and enhance reusability.
  • Implement Error Handlers: Apply flow-level handlers, action-specific conditions, and Try logic to capture diagnostics, notify admins, and allow recovery without halting the entire process.
  • Leverage Decision Tables: Replace complex if-else logic with visual tables for routing approvals or assignments based on CI attributes or incident priority.
  • Automate Incident Routing: Combine machine learning categorization with CMDB relationships to prioritize, assign, and notify based on CI ownership dynamically.
  • Build Incrementally with Testing: Develop flows iteratively, testing success and error paths in a safe environment before production deployment to minimize risks.

Consider this Flow Designer example for high-priority incident email notifications: Trigger on Incident creation where priority is 1 (Critical), then use Send Email action with data pills from the incident record to notify the assignment group.

// Simulated Flow Designer logic in script step
var grInc = new GlideRecord('incident');
grInc.addQuery('priority', 1);
grInc.query();
while (grInc.next()) {
  gs.eventQueue('incident.high.priority', grInc, 'assigned_to', gs.getUserID());
}

For a practical ITSM use case, automate user onboarding via a Service Catalog trigger: Submit catalog item, seek manager approval, create sys_user record, assign to CI groups from CMDB, and update requested-for fields—all orchestrated in one flow with subflows for provisioning.

Integrating CMDB with Flow Designer for ITSM Efficiency

Combining CMDB accuracy with Flow Designer unlocks advanced ITSM automation, such as impact analysis during changes or automated routing using CI dependencies.

Example script within a Flow Designer action to route incidents by CMDB-owned group:

var grInc = new GlideRecord('incident');
if (grInc.get(current.sys_id)) {
  var ci = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci');
  if (ci.get(grInc.cmdb_ci)) {
    grInc.assignment_group = ci.owned_by;
    grInc.update();
  }
}

This integration ensures decisions are data-driven, reducing MTTR (Mean Time to Resolution) by proactively identifying affected services via CMDB relationships.

Conclusion: Achieving ITSM Excellence

By maintaining a precise CMDB and optimizing workflows with Flow Designer, organizations achieve proactive, efficient ITSM operations aligned with ITIL, delivering faster resolutions and superior service quality.

title: Flow Designer Transaction Boundaries: What Every ServiceNow Developer Must Know
excerpt: Flow Designer executes asynchronously with no native rollback. Learn how transactions commit, when to use business rules instead, and proven compensating transaction patterns.
content:
Understanding Flow Designer's Execution Model

Flow Designer typically runs asynchronously relative to the record write that triggered it. That means the triggering database transaction commits first, then the flow runs in a separate execution context. The important implication: there is no single, multi-step database transaction spanning all actions inside a flow.

What This Means in Practice

Each action that writes to the database commits independently. If a later step fails (integration timeout, missing data, unexpected state), earlier updates are already committed.

// Typical flow timeline (conceptual)
// 1) Trigger: Incident created (record commit happens)
// 2) Action: Update CI (commits)
// 3) Action: Create Task (commits)
// 4) Action: REST call fails
// Result: CI update + Task are already in the database

When to Use Business Rules Instead

If you need logic to run inside the same database transaction as the record write, Flow Designer is usually the wrong tool. A Before Business Rule runs before the record is committed, allowing you to validate and set values safely.

ScenarioUse Business RuleUse Flow Designer
Must run before DB write✓ Before BR✗
Same transaction required✓ Before/After BR (carefully)✗
Long-running process✗✓ Async
Multi-step orchestration✗✓
External integrations with retries✗✓

Production Patterns That Work

1) Compensating Transactions

Instead of rollback, you implement a deliberate "undo" step if something fails: close the task you created, revert a field, write an audit note, etc.

2) Idempotency

Design actions so re-running them does not duplicate work. For example, create tasks with a unique key (incident + purpose) and check if it already exists before creating a new one.

3) State Machines Over "Do Everything At Once"

For complex workflows, store a state on the record (or a related orchestration table) and advance it step-by-step. This makes retries safe and failures diagnosable.

Minimal Example: Safe Task Creation

// Prevent duplicate tasks (idempotent create)
var t = new GlideRecord('task');
t.addQuery('parent', current.getUniqueValue());
t.addQuery('short_description', 'Follow-up approval');
t.setLimit(1);
t.query();
if (!t.next()) {
  t.initialize();
  t.parent = current.getUniqueValue();
  t.short_description = 'Follow-up approval';
  t.insert();
}

Conclusion

Flow Designer is excellent for orchestration, but it is not a database transaction manager. Treat every write as "committed forever", design for retries, and use compensating patterns when you need consistency across steps.

title: Scoped Application Security Patterns: Cross-Scope Access Done Right
excerpt: Navigate ServiceNow's scoped application security model with confidence. Learn cross-scope access patterns, ACL evaluation order, and security best practices.
content:
Why Scoped Security Trips Teams Up

In scoped applications, security is not just ACLs. You also have to manage cross-scope behavior: which app can call which APIs, and which app can access which tables. The goal is safe reuse without accidentally granting broad access.

ACL Evaluation Order

ACLs evaluate from most specific to least specific:

  1. Field-level on specific table
  2. Table-level on specific table
  3. Field-level wildcard
  4. Table-level wildcard

GlideRecordSecure vs GlideRecord

// GlideRecordSecure automatically enforces ACLs
var grs = new GlideRecordSecure('incident');
grs.query();
while (grs.next()) {
  // Only returns records user can read
}

// GlideRecord requires manual checks
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
  if (gr.canRead()) {
    // Safe to display
  }
}

Cross-Scope Access: Practical Patterns

1) Prefer Application Access on Tables

If a scoped app must read/write another app's table, start with table-level Application Access settings (and keep it as narrow as possible).

2) Use Explicit Cross-Scope Privileges

When a scoped app needs to call an API in another scope, define explicit privileges instead of broad global access. This creates an audit trail and prevents accidental dependency creep.

3) Keep Client-Callable Surface Area Small

Client-callable Script Includes increase your attack surface. Expose only the exact methods needed, validate inputs, and return minimal data.

Security Anti-Patterns to Avoid

  • Using session tricks to bypass ACLs
  • Hardcoding admin credentials in integrations
  • Making all Script Includes client-callable
  • Storing sensitive data in client-accessible fields
  • Using eval() or dynamic script execution

Conclusion

Good scoped security is about intentional boundaries: least-privilege ACLs, explicit cross-scope permissions, and minimal client-callable exposure. If you can explain your access model in one diagram, you're probably doing it right.

title: Predictive Intelligence Deep Dive: Requirements, Limitations, and Production Patterns
excerpt: Predictive Intelligence requires minimum 10,000 records for classification training. Learn the real requirements, common misconceptions, and patterns for production ML implementations.
content:
Predictive Intelligence Components

Predictive Intelligence is a set of ML capabilities that learn from historical data to recommend or predict values on new records.

  • Classification: Auto-categorization / assignment recommendations
  • Similarity: Find related records ("tickets like this")
  • Clustering: Discover hidden groupings / patterns
  • Regression: Predict numeric values

Critical Training Requirements

Classification requires a minimum of 10,000 records for training. In real production implementations, more data typically improves coverage and stability.

Model TypeMinimum RecordsRecommended
Classification10,00050,000+
Similarity1,00010,000+
Clustering5,00025,000+

Data Quality: The Real Make-or-Break

  • Label consistency: assignment group/category values must be stable (avoid frequent renames)
  • Noise reduction: remove misrouted tickets from the training set
  • Class balance: if one group owns 90% of tickets, your model will look "accurate" but be useless

Common Misconception: Major Incident Prediction

Major incident detection commonly uses similarity models to find tickets similar to existing major incidents—it does not magically predict brand new categories of major incidents with no precedent.

Production Patterns

1) Human-in-the-loop rollouts

Start with recommendations (not auto-updates). Let agents accept/reject. Use that feedback to clean labels and retrain.

2) Guardrails

Only apply predictions when confidence is above a threshold, and always log when the system changed a value automatically.

3) Retraining cadence

Plan retraining when org structure changes (new teams, major routing changes) and when ticket distributions drift.

Simple Example: Applying a Predicted Group Safely

// Example: apply predicted group only when present
if (!current.assignment_group.nil() || current.u_predicted_group.nil()) {
  return;
}

current.assignment_group = current.u_predicted_group;
current.work_notes = 'Assignment set by Predictive Intelligence recommendation.';

Conclusion

Predictive Intelligence is strongest when your data is clean and your operating model is stable. Treat it like a product: curate the dataset, roll out gradually, and measure outcomes (MTTR, reassignment rates, and acceptance rate) instead of chasing accuracy alone.

title: Yokohama MFA Enforcement: What You Need to Know Before Upgrading
excerpt: Multi-factor authentication is mandatory in Yokohama with a 90-day grace period. Here's everything you need to configure before upgrading.
content:
Critical Breaking Change

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enabled and required by default for all local login users starting with the Yokohama release. This mandatory enforcement applies to internal users without the snc_external role using local or LDAP authentication, adding an essential security layer to protect your ServiceNow instance.

What is Multi-Factor Authentication?

MFA requires users to provide two or more verification factors to gain access to the instance, such as something they know (password) and something they have (authenticator app code). This significantly reduces the risk of unauthorized access from compromised credentials. ServiceNow supports authenticator apps like Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator that generate time-based one-time passwords (TOTP).

90-Day Grace Period Details

For the first 90 days after upgrading to Yokohama, internal users (without snc_external role) logging in with local or LDAP authentication can access the instance normally but must enroll in MFA within 30 days of their first successful login. Users will see a prominent enrollment prompt during login. After 30 days, MFA becomes mandatory for login. After the full 90 days, MFA enforcement is strict with no self-enrollment grace period for new logins—admins can extend this up to 270 days if needed.

Pre-Upgrade Checklist

  1. Audit current authentication and identify all local login users
  2. Configure MFA policies before upgrade
  3. Test in non-production environments
  4. Communicate to users 2-4 weeks in advance
  5. Prepare support team for MFA-related tickets
  6. Review and set exemptions as needed
var users = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
users.addActiveQuery();
users.addQuery('source', 'NULL').addOrCondition('source', '');
